stem: A container app must read blobs using its managed identity. Which role assignment grants data-plane read access?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader
Reader
Storage Account Contributor
Contributor

explanation: Storage separates control plane from data plane. Only the Storage Blob Data roles grant access to blob contents; the generic management roles grant access to the account resource, not the data inside it.

whyWrong.B: Reader shows the account exists and lets you read its properties. It cannot read a blob.
whyWrong.C: Storage Account Contributor manages the account and can read keys, but grants no direct data-plane access under RBAC.
whyWrong.D: Contributor is broad management access and, again, not a data-plane role.

docs.title: Assign an Azure role for blob data access

stem: A team needs to give an external partner time-limited read access to one blob container, without an Entra identity. What is appropriate?

options.text: A short-lived user delegation SAS on the container
The storage account access key
Anonymous public read access on the container
A Contributor role assignment on the storage account

explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with Entra ID credentials rather than the account key, so it can be revoked by revoking the delegation key and it carries the signer's permissions as a ceiling. Scope and expiry limit the blast radius.

whyWrong.B: The account key grants full control of everything in the account and cannot be scoped or expired.
whyWrong.C: Public access removes authentication for everyone, not just the partner.
whyWrong.D: That requires the partner to have an identity in your directory and grants far too much.

hint: The partner has no Entra identity, so it needs a token in the URL - but you still want it signed by a real identity and short-lived.

stem: Which App Configuration feature lets you roll out and instantly withdraw a change without redeploying?

options.text: Feature flags via `IFeatureManager`
Labels on the key-values
Snapshots of the store
Key Vault references in the store

explanation: Feature flags exist to separate deploy from release. The code ships with the feature behind a flag, and the flag can be flipped — including by percentage or audience — without touching the deployment.

whyWrong.B: Labels distinguish values per environment; they are not a runtime toggle.
whyWrong.C: Snapshots capture an immutable point-in-time set of configuration.
whyWrong.D: Key Vault references resolve secrets and have nothing to do with rollout.

stem: An app reads configuration from App Configuration at startup only. Operations need a connection timeout changed without a restart. What is missing?

options.text: A sentinel key with a cache expiration
A second App Configuration store
Geo-replication of the config store
A Key Vault reference for the timeout value

explanation: The provider only re-reads when refresh is configured. Registering a sentinel key with a cache expiration makes the app poll that one key and reload everything when it changes — which is also why the sentinel is updated last, after the real values.

whyWrong.B: A second store adds no refresh behaviour.
whyWrong.C: Geo-replication improves availability and latency, not refresh.
whyWrong.D: A timeout is not a secret, and Key Vault references do not add dynamic refresh.

hint: Reading at startup only means nothing is watching for changes. Ask what registration makes the client poll, and what it should watch.

stem: Which statement about a system-assigned managed identity is correct when the resource is deleted and recreated?

options.text: A new identity with a new object id is created
The same identity is restored along with its role assignments
The identity survives in the directory and can be reattached
Role assignments transfer automatically to the new identity

explanation: A system-assigned identity shares its resource's lifecycle. Recreating the resource produces a brand-new service principal, so every role assignment must be granted again — which is the main reason infrastructure that is torn down and rebuilt tends to use a user-assigned identity instead.

whyWrong.B: The old identity is deleted with the resource.
whyWrong.C: It is removed from the directory, not orphaned for reattachment.
whyWrong.D: Assignments reference the old object id and become stale.

stem: A secret must be rotated every 60 days with no downtime for running apps. Which combination achieves this?

options.text: Apps read the versionless URI and a policy rotates it
Apps pin the secret version and are redeployed after each rotation
Apps read the secret on every request so they always have the newest value
Purge protection is enabled so old versions remain available

explanation: The versionless URI means callers always resolve the current version, so writing a new one is transparent. The rotation policy plus a `SecretNearExpiry` event gives you the automation trigger without a scheduled job of your own.

whyWrong.B: Pinning the version guarantees a redeploy is needed for every rotation, which is the downtime being avoided.
whyWrong.C: Per-request reads get throttled and are the documented anti-pattern; cache with periodic refresh instead.
whyWrong.D: Purge protection governs deletion, not rotation.

hint: Apps must not have to learn the new version. Ask what URI form avoids pinning a version, and what raises the event that triggers rotation.

stem: Which Key Vault role allows an application to read secret values but not create, update or delete them?

options.text: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Reader
Key Vault Secrets Officer
Key Vault Crypto User

explanation: Secrets User grants get and list on secret values — the minimum an application needs.

whyWrong.B: Key Vault Reader can see vault and secret metadata but cannot read secret values.
whyWrong.C: Secrets Officer can also write and delete, exceeding read-only.
whyWrong.D: Crypto User covers key operations such as sign and unwrap, not secrets.

stem: For each requirement, choose where the value belongs.

choices.text: An app setting in plain text

blanks.label: The retrieval top-K, tuned per environment
A percentage rollout of a new ranking model

explanation: Key Vault is for secrets, where auditing, rotation and tight RBAC matter and per-transaction cost is acceptable. App Configuration is for everything else — non-secret settings, separated per environment by labels, plus feature flags for gradual rollout. Using a managed identity, App Configuration can also hold Key Vault references so the application reads one source.

docs.title: Use Key Vault references in App Configuration

hint: Sort by what the value is: a credential, a tuneable setting, or something toggled per audience.

stem: Which approach removes credentials from a GitHub Actions workflow that deploys to Azure?

options.text: OpenID Connect federation from the workflow
Storing a service principal secret as a repository secret
Storing the publish profile as a repository secret
Using a personal access token with Contributor rights

explanation: With a federated credential on the app registration trusting the workflow's OIDC issuer, subject and audience, the runner exchanges its short-lived token for an Azure access token. Nothing long-lived is stored in the repository.

whyWrong.B: A client secret is exactly the stored credential being eliminated, and it expires.
whyWrong.C: A publish profile embeds credentials.
whyWrong.D: A PAT is a long-lived credential with broad rights.

stem: An app authenticates locally with the Azure CLI and in Azure with a user-assigned managed identity, but fails in Azure with an error about multiple identities. What is wrong?

options.text: Several identities attached and no client id given
`DefaultAzureCredential` cannot be used with user-assigned identities
The Azure CLI credential takes priority in Azure
The identity is missing the Reader role

explanation: With more than one user-assigned identity attached, the request is ambiguous and the token provider cannot choose. Passing the client id — through the credential options or the `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` setting — resolves it. A system-assigned identity needs no such hint.

whyWrong.B: It supports them; it just needs to be told which one.
whyWrong.C: The CLI credential sits late in the chain and is not available on a deployed host anyway.
whyWrong.D: A missing role produces an authorisation failure, not an ambiguous-identity error.

hint: The credential chain found more than one candidate and cannot choose. Ask what you must tell it.

stem: Which practice most reduces the impact of a leaked application credential?

options.text: Replacing it with a managed identity
Rotating it every twelve months
Storing it in an environment variable rather than a config file
Encoding it as base64 before storing it

explanation: The strongest control is eliminating the credential. A managed identity has no secret to store, copy or leak, and its tokens are short-lived and issued by the platform.

whyWrong.B: Annual rotation leaves a very long window of exposure.
whyWrong.C: Environment variables are still readable by anything running in the process context.
whyWrong.D: Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and offers no protection at all.

stem: You need to know how long the embedding call takes as a share of total request time, per request. Which instrumentation gives you that?

options.text: A custom span around the embedding call
A counter metric incremented per embedding call
A log entry written before and after the call
A histogram of total request duration

explanation: A child span carries its own start and end within the parent trace, so the end-to-end view shows exactly how much of each request the embedding call accounted for. Metrics aggregate across requests and cannot answer a per-request question.

whyWrong.B: A counter tells you how many calls happened, not how long they took.
whyWrong.C: Paired log lines can be correlated by hand but produce no structured duration in the transaction view.
whyWrong.D: Total duration does not attribute time to the embedding step.

hint: You want the embedding call measured as its own segment inside the request, so the two durations can be compared on one timeline.

stem: Which KQL operator combines rows from two tables into one result set without correlating them?

options.text: `union`
`join`
`lookup`
`mv-expand`

explanation: `union` stacks rows from several tables, which is how you scan requests, dependencies and exceptions together before filtering on a shared field such as `operation_Id`.

whyWrong.B: `join` matches rows on a key and produces combined rows.
whyWrong.C: `lookup` enriches from a dimension table, a specialised join.
whyWrong.D: `mv-expand` flattens an array within a single row.

stem: Ingestion costs are dominated by verbose dependency telemetry from a chatty internal service, but you must keep full fidelity for checkout requests. What do you configure?

options.text: Sampling that keeps all checkout traces
A daily ingestion cap on the workspace
A shorter workspace retention period
Disabling dependency collection entirely

explanation: Sampling with a rule that always keeps the important operation gives you cost control without losing the traces that matter. Because sampling decisions apply to whole traces, the retained checkout traces stay complete.

whyWrong.B: A cap stops ingestion once reached, leaving you blind for the rest of the day — including for checkout.
whyWrong.C: Retention affects storage cost rather than ingestion volume.
whyWrong.D: Dropping all dependencies removes exactly the spans that make a trace diagnosable.

hint: You need less data overall but full fidelity for one operation. That rules out a flat percentage applied to everything.

stem: Which signal type should record the number of tokens consumed per model call, for dashboards and alerting over time?

options.text: A metric, aggregated cheaply at collection time
A log entry per call, carrying the token count as a property
A span attribute, recorded on the span for that model call
A custom event per call, with the token count as a dimension

explanation: Metrics are aggregated at collection time, so they stay cheap to store and fast to query across long windows — the right choice for a value you want to chart and alert on. Recording it as a span attribute too is useful for per-request debugging.

whyWrong.B: Per-call logs are expensive at volume and slow to aggregate over months.
whyWrong.C: Span attributes are excellent for one request but are subject to sampling and are not pre-aggregated.
whyWrong.D: Custom events have the same volume and cost profile as logs.

stem: Which KQL clause makes a text search fastest over a large log table?

options.text: `where Message has "timeout"`
`where Message contains "timeout"`
`search "timeout"`
`where Message matches regex "timeout"`

explanation: `has` matches whole terms using the term index, so it can skip data without scanning. `contains` performs a substring scan and regex is slower still, while a bare `search` scans every column of every table.

whyWrong.B: Substring matching cannot use the term index.
whyWrong.C: `search` without a table is the most expensive form of all.
whyWrong.D: Regular expressions are evaluated per row with no index support.

stem: An alert must fire only if failures exceed a threshold in three consecutive evaluations, to avoid paging on a single blip. Which alert setting provides this?

options.text: The number of violations in a window
A longer query time range on the rule
A higher severity level on the alert
An action group with a delay set

explanation: Log search alert rules let you require several violations before firing, so a transient spike is ignored while a sustained problem still pages. It is the standard control for alert noise.

whyWrong.B: A longer window smooths the data but still fires on the first evaluation that crosses the threshold.
whyWrong.C: Severity changes routing and urgency, not the firing condition.
whyWrong.D: Action groups decide who is notified, not whether the rule fires.

hint: You want repeated breaches, not a single spike. Ask which alert setting counts violations before firing.

stem: Requests to a downstream service intermittently fail and Application Insights shows them as dependency failures with result code 429. What is the appropriate first response in the calling code?

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Retry immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds
Treat it as fatal and fail the user's request
Increase the client's timeout setting

explanation: 429 means the service is asking you to slow down. Backoff with jitter spreads retries so clients do not resynchronise into a thundering herd, and honouring retry-after respects the service's own guidance.

whyWrong.B: Immediate retries add load to an already-throttled service and make recovery slower.
whyWrong.C: 429 is explicitly transient and retryable.
whyWrong.D: The call is being rejected quickly, not running slowly.

stem: A distributed trace shows a 3-second gap between the API span ending and the worker span starting. What does this most likely represent?

options.text: Time the message spent queued
Clock skew between the two hosts
A failed retry that was not recorded
Sampling dropping the intermediate spans

explanation: In an asynchronous hand-off the gap is queue latency — the message waited for a consumer. Seeing it explicitly is one of the main reasons to propagate trace context through the queue, since it distinguishes a slow worker from a backed-up queue.

whyWrong.B: Skew is possible but usually small, and would shift spans rather than produce a consistent gap.
whyWrong.C: A failed retry would normally appear as its own failed span.
whyWrong.D: Sampling keeps or drops whole traces, so it would not remove only the middle.

hint: Neither service was busy during the gap. Ask what sat between them and what the work was doing during that time.

stem: Choose the table that answers each question.

blanks.label: Which incoming HTTP requests failed in the last hour?
Which outbound calls to Cosmos DB were slow?
What did the application log while handling a request?

explanation: requests covers work coming in, dependencies covers calls going out, traces holds `ILogger` output and exceptions holds thrown errors. All four share `operation_Id`, which is what lets you union them and reconstruct a single operation end to end.

stem: Which resource attribute should differ between replicas of the same service so you can tell instances apart?

options.text: `service.instance.id`
`service.name`
`service.version`
`deployment.environment`

explanation: `service.name` identifies the logical service and should be identical across replicas, becoming `cloud_RoleName`. `service.instance.id` distinguishes the individual replica and becomes `cloud_RoleInstance`, which is what lets you spot one bad instance.

whyWrong.B: Varying it per replica would fragment the application map into many false services.
whyWrong.C: Version identifies the release, which is normally the same across replicas.
whyWrong.D: Environment is the same for every replica in that environment.

stem: After enabling the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro, traces appear but the application's `ILogger` output does not. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The logging provider is not wired up
The distro exports traces and metrics but never log records
The connection string is missing the log ingestion endpoint
Sampling is discarding the log records before they are exported

explanation: The distro covers traces, metrics and logs, but log records still pass through the normal logging pipeline — so a minimum level set above the entries being written, or a provider that was never registered, produces exactly this asymmetry.

whyWrong.B: Logs are one of the three signals the distro handles.
whyWrong.C: An invalid connection string would stop traces arriving as well.
whyWrong.D: Sampling reduces volume proportionally rather than eliminating a signal.

hint: Traces arrive, so the exporter and connection string are fine. That narrows it to how logs specifically are collected and filtered.

stem: Put the steps of diagnosing a user-reported slow request in the order that gets to the cause fastest.

options.text: Find the request in `requests` and note its `operation_Id`
Union `requests`, `dependencies` and `exceptions` filtered on that `operation_Id`
Identify which dependency span accounts for most of the duration
Query that dependency's own telemetry to see whether it is slow for everyone or just this call

explanation: Start from the specific complaint and widen only as needed. The correlation id reconstructs the whole operation, the span durations point at the culprit, and only then is it worth asking whether the problem is systemic — which decides whether you are fixing one caller or a shared dependency.
hint: Start from the one request the user complained about, get its correlation id, then widen to everything sharing that id before drawing conclusions.
